# Button

Figma: [02a. Button](https://www.figma.com/design/a7Z956YZy9n6f9uz5DK16Y?node-id=69-889) · Family: 02 Actions · Status: stable · Version 2.0.0 · Updated 2026-05-19

The Button is the primary action component of the Safqah design system. It signals what users can do, how important an action is, and how the system responds. Buttons appear in onboarding flows, transactional moments, modals, lists, and forms - so they're built to scale across 6 visual variants, 3 sizes, 6 states, both LTR and RTL directions, and optional leading/trailing icons.

Reference image (every variant, labelled): `knowledge/examples/components/button/reference.png`

### Button

The labelled action control that every transactional moment in Safqah routes through (invest, reserve, withdraw, confirm, cancel). Six variants encode how loud and how risky the action is.

Level: organism · Part of: ButtonGroup

Use when:
- The single main action of a screen or sheet, such as «استثمر الآن» on a deal page or «تأكيد» in an investment confirmation: Variant=primary, Size=lg
- The escape or alternative action next to a primary (Cancel, Back): Variant=secondary
- Irreversible actions such as withdrawing before maturity or deleting an account, always behind a confirmation: Variant=destructive
- Submit blocked by validation errors or a Retry after a failed request: Variant=error

Don't use when:
- The click moves the user to another route or URL (terms, Learn more, Forgot password as navigation): use Link
- The action is a universally understood icon with no label (close, share, copy): use IconButton
- Two or three related actions must sit together with set spacing and order: wrap them in ButtonGroup
- Signing in with Nafath, Apple or Google: use SocialButton
- A persistent screen-level action floating over scroll content: use FAB / Standard or FAB / Extended

Accessibility: At most one primary per screen; sm (32px) is below the 44pt touch target, so keep lg or md on mobile and block taps while State=loading to avoid duplicate investment submissions.

## Guide from the doc page

### Overview

A Button is a control that triggers an immediate action when activated. It is the most-used component in the Safqah system - every transactional moment (invest, withdraw, confirm, cancel) routes through one. Because of this, the Button is the most carefully tested component, both for visual consistency and accessibility.

Button v2 ships with 216 explicit variant combinations across 6 visual variants, 3 sizes, 6 states, and 2 directions (LTR and RTL). This explicit coverage exists for design documentation and exploration. At Flutter runtime, State is collapsed automatically into gesture handling and Direction into the Directionality widget - engineering consumes Variant + Size as explicit parameters and the rest comes from system context.

### Live preview - one of each variant

### Anatomy

A Button has three structural slots arranged horizontally: a leading icon slot, a label, and a trailing icon slot. Both icon slots are independently toggleable via boolean properties. The label is always present and is the primary content of the button. When State is loading, the label slot displays three dots and icon slots are visually hidden.

**1. Leading icon**
Optional 16/20/24px icon (sm/md/lg). Toggled via Has icon leading. Swappable via Icon leading property - defaults to placeholder, overridden in product to a real icon from the Syntropy Icons library.

**2. Label**
Always present. Bound to the Label property - overridable per instance from the right panel. Typography: Medium weight at 13/14/16px (sm/md/lg).

**3. Trailing icon**
Optional, mirrors leading icon behavior. Common in disclosure buttons (with chevron-right), download triggers (with download icon), or external link buttons (with arrow-up-right).

### Variants

Six visual variants cover the affordance hierarchy a typical Safqah screen needs. Each variant has a clear semantic meaning - pick the one that matches the user's intent, not the visual look you want. Mixing variants on one screen should be intentional: usually one primary action, optionally one secondary or tertiary, and any text/destructive/error variants used sparingly.

| Primary Solid green fill with white label. The highest-affordance button - visually the loudest action on the screen. Built on bg/brand/primary with text/on-brand. Pressed and hover states darken to bg/brand/primary-pressed and bg/brand/primary-hover. | When to use The single most important action in a flow - Invest, Confirm, Submit. Limit one per screen. If you have two equally-weighted actions, both should NOT be primary; the lesser one becomes secondary. |
| --- | --- |

| Secondary Transparent fill with a green outline and green label. Visually quieter than primary but still clearly actionable. On hover/pressed, the fill becomes bg/brand/primary-subtle (very faint green) to confirm interaction. | When to use The supporting action that lives next to a primary - Cancel next to Confirm, Back next to Continue. Also good as a standalone CTA in less critical surfaces (filter menus, secondary screens). |
| --- | --- |

| Tertiary Subtle green-tinted fill with dark default text. Designed deliberately to NOT use brand green for the label - pairing bg/brand/primary-subtle with text/default yields ~14:1 contrast (AAA), unlike the green-on-green that would fail WCAG. | When to use A button that should feel "available but quiet" - embedded actions in cards, list-row actions, optional steps. Use when neither primary nor secondary is right because both still pull too much attention. |
| --- | --- |

| Destructive Solid red fill (bg/error) with white label. Reserved for actions that delete, withdraw, or irreversibly change state. The red is intentionally loud - it should give the user pause before they click. | When to use Deleting an account, canceling a subscription, withdrawing funds before maturity, removing a verified document. Pair with a confirmation dialog whenever the action is non-undoable. |
| --- | --- |

| Error Subtle red fill (bg/error-subtle) with red text and red outline. Visually announces "this action exists but something is wrong with it" - for buttons attached to invalid forms, expired sessions, or actions blocked by validation. | When to use A "Submit" button under a form with validation errors. A "Retry" button on a failed API call. A button that signals "the system noticed a problem with this action" but still offers the user a path forward. |
| --- | --- |

| Text No fill, no border, green label only. The lowest-affordance button - barely distinguishable from regular text until hovered. Hover/pressed states add a subtle bg/brand/primary-subtle background to confirm clickability. | When to use Inline links inside body copy that need to be buttons rather than navigation links (e.g. "Show more" toggles). Tertiary actions in densely packed lists where any chrome would feel heavy. Use sparingly - they're easy to miss. |
| --- | --- |

### Sizes

Three sizes cover density across surfaces: lg for marketing pages, full-screen modals, and hero CTAs; md as the default for most product UI; sm for dense lists, inline actions in cards, and toolbar buttons. Size affects height, padding, font size, icon size, and gap simultaneously - they scale together so proportions stay consistent.

### States

Six states cover the interaction lifecycle. In Flutter, State is collapsed automatically - gesture detection toggles default → hover → pressed, focus traversal triggers focused, and the Loading prop triggers loading. Designers only need to think about these explicitly when documenting flows or specifying disabled rules.

Default

Resting state. No user interaction.

Hover

Cursor is over the button (desktop/web only). Background shifts to primary-hover. Not rendered on Flutter mobile (no hover events).

Pressed

Button is being actively clicked/tapped. Background shifts to primary-pressed. Brief visual feedback.

Focused

Button has keyboard focus. A 2px outline (border/focus → text/default for max contrast) wraps the button, visible against any background.

Disabled

Button cannot be activated. Background and text shift to disabled tokens. Pointer events are blocked at the Flutter runtime level.

Loading

Async action is in progress. The label is replaced with three dots; icons are hidden. Pointer events are blocked.

### Direction - LTR and RTL

Safqah serves Arabic-speaking users by default. Every Button variant has an explicit RTL twin where the icon order is mirrored (trailing icon visually appears on the left, leading icon on the right) but the slots keep their semantic names. This means a "leading icon" remains the icon that signals "before" relative to reading direction - visually left in LTR, visually right in RTL.

In production, Flutter handles direction automatically. When the app is wrapped in Directionality(textDirection: TextDirection.rtl), all buttons mirror without code changes - engineering does not need to import a separate RTL component. The RTL variants in this file exist for design documentation, prototyping Arabic flows, and reviewing mirror behavior at design-time.

LTR - Left-to-right

Icon-leading sits on the visual left, icon-trailing on the visual right. Used for English, French, and all other LTR scripts. This is the default direction.

RTL - Right-to-left

Icon-leading sits on the visual right, icon-trailing on the visual left - the slots keep their semantic names ("leading" still means "before in reading order"). Used for Arabic, Hebrew, Urdu, Farsi.

> **Info:** For your Flutter implementation: wrap your app or any subtree in Directionality(textDirection: ...) and the button will mirror its children automatically using its HORIZONTAL auto-layout. You do not need to pick a "Direction" variant in code - that property exists for Figma documentation only.

> **Tip:** When designing in Figma, use the Direction variant explicitly when mocking Arabic screens. Set the Label property to your Arabic copy (e.g. "ابدأ الاستثمار" or "تأكيد"). The dots in the loading state remain "• • •" regardless of direction.

### Icons

Buttons support an optional leading icon (visually before the label in reading direction) and an optional trailing icon (visually after). Both icons are independent and can be combined - a button can have neither, leading only, trailing only, or both.

Two component properties control each icon: a Boolean (Has icon leading / Has icon trailing) that toggles visibility, and an Instance Swap (Icon leading / Icon trailing) that picks which icon to display. The default instance is a placeholder green square - in production it gets swapped to a real icon from the Syntropy Icons library.

Large button

Icon: 24px · Button height: 48px

Medium button (default)

Icon: 20px · Button height: 40px

Small button

Icon: 16px · Button height: 32px

Why three icon sizes: button heights are 32/40/48px, and the icon needs to read as proportional within that space - too small and the icon disappears, too large and it crowds the label. The 16/20/24 scale follows a common ratio: icon height is roughly half the button height. The icon visually occupies the same proportional space across all three sizes.

> **Warning:** Always pick icons from the Syntropy Icons library - never paste in custom SVGs. The Icons library handles stroke width, optical alignment, and 2-mode theming. A pasted SVG will look wrong in dark mode and won't scale cleanly across the three button sizes.

### Code examples

How engineering consumes the Button. Each language tab shows the same example - a primary medium button labeled "Invest now" with an onPressed handler.

### Flutter / Dart

```dart
SafqahButton(
  label: 'Invest now',
  variant: SafqahButtonVariant.primary,
  size: SafqahButtonSize.md,
  leadingIcon: SafqahIcons.arrowRight,
  onPressed: () => _handleInvest(),
)

// Loading state
SafqahButton(
  label: 'Invest now',
  variant: SafqahButtonVariant.primary,
  isLoading: _submitting,
  onPressed: _submitting ? null : () => _handleInvest(),
)

// RTL - wrap in Directionality
Directionality(
  textDirection: TextDirection.rtl,
  child: SafqahButton(
    label: 'استثمر الآن',
    variant: SafqahButtonVariant.primary,
    onPressed: () => _handleInvest(),
  ),
)
```

### React / TypeScript (web prototype only)

```typescript
<Button
  label="Invest now"
  variant="primary"
  size="md"
  leadingIcon={<ArrowRightIcon />}
  onClick={handleInvest}
/>

// Loading state
<Button
  label="Invest now"
  variant="primary"
  isLoading={submitting}
  disabled={submitting}
  onClick={handleInvest}
/>

// RTL - set dir on a parent or via the document
<div dir="rtl">
  <Button label="استثمر الآن" variant="primary" onClick={handleInvest} />
</div>
```

### Usage - Do and Don't

Concrete patterns to follow and avoid. These rules are derived from real Safqah screens and from the consequences of the variant choices already documented.

- **Do** · Scenario · Investment confirmation modal: One primary for the main action, one secondary for the escape hatch. The user instantly knows which button moves them forward and which one backs them out.
- **Don't** · Scenario · Investment confirmation modal: Two primaries fighting for attention. The user has to read both labels to decide which is the actual main action - and many will pick the wrong one or none at all.
- **Do** · Scenario · Account deletion confirmation: Red destructive on the dangerous action, neutral secondary on the safe one. The red gives the user a half-second of pause - exactly what an irreversible action needs.
- **Don't** · Scenario · Account deletion confirmation: Green primary on a destructive action reads as "safe to proceed" - the user clicks faster than they should. Use destructive (red) for anything that destroys data.
- **Do** · Scenario · Portfolio card - row action: A tertiary sm button blends into the card chrome. It's available when the user reaches for it but doesn't compete with the portfolio numbers above it.
- **Don't** · Scenario · Portfolio card - row action: A solid green primary inside a list row screams for attention louder than the portfolio value above it. Users will click before they've absorbed the data - wrong moment, wrong button.
- **Do** · Scenario · Wizard step footer: Both buttons at lg. Even visual weight on both - the user can grab either one without their eye having to recalibrate. Matched sizes = matched importance.
- **Don't** · Scenario · Wizard step footer: Mixed sizes in the same footer row. The eye reads "Back" as a side-note when it should be a peer action. Worse: a user wanting to go back has to hunt for the smaller target.
- **Do** · Scenario · Form submit with validation errors: Error variant says "this action exists but something is wrong" - the red outline mirrors the field-level errors above. User understands: fix the fields, then try again.
- **Don't** · Scenario · Form submit with validation errors: Destructive red on a submit button reads as "submitting will damage something." Wrong tone - the form is blocked, not dangerous. Use error variant for validation states.
- **Do** · Scenario · Login form - secondary path: Text variant reads as a link, which is exactly what "Forgot password?" is - a navigation, not a primary action. Sits inline with the form without competing with Sign in.
- **Don't** · Scenario · Login form - secondary path: Solid green primary on a recovery flow makes "Forgot password?" look as important as the main login button. Users get visually confused about which to click first.

### Notes from the maintainer

Six short notes summarizing the most important things the team should remember about the Button. Treat these as the "what people get wrong" cheat sheet.

> **Info:** Why buttons matter: the Button is the most-used component in the system. Every transactional moment routes through one. A 5% improvement in button affordance compounds across thousands of daily flows - this is why we spent 216 variants getting it right.

> **Tip:** Choosing the right variant: ask "what does the user need to do with this button, and how loud should it feel?" - not "what does it look like?" Primary = the most important. Secondary = the alternative. Tertiary = quiet but available. Destructive = will cause damage. Error = blocked by validation. Text = barely visible chrome.

> **Info:** Working with icons: always pull from the Syntropy Icons library. Icons are themed for light and dark mode there - pasted SVGs are not. Match icon size to button size (16/20/24). If you need an icon-only button, use 02b. IconButton instead.

> **Warning:** Anti-patterns we keep seeing: (1) two primary buttons side by side - pick one. (2) destructive used for "Cancel" - that's a navigation, not a destruction. (3) tertiary used as a hero CTA - users will miss it. (4) custom colors instead of variants - every color decision lives in a token, not in your file.

> **Info:** RTL implementation: at Flutter runtime, the Directionality widget mirrors all HORIZONTAL auto-layout children automatically - engineering does NOT pick the RTL variant explicitly. The RTL variants in Figma exist for design-time documentation, prototyping, and reviewing Arabic flows. In code, your widget tree contains one SafqahButton, not SafqahButtonLTR and SafqahButtonRTL.

> **Tip:** External resources to internalize: Material 3 buttons doc for variant hierarchy reasoning, WCAG 1.4.3 and 1.4.11 for the contrast math, Apple HIG for the touch target rule (44pt). The other internal links lead to the Syntropy Icons library and Safqah Brand kit - both are required reading before customizing button content.
